meta.title: Vietnamese A1 Beginner
meta.subtitle: 500 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Vietnamese → English (see the Vietnamese, recall the meaning) and English → Vietnamese (see an English meaning, recall the Vietnamese). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 500 words for a beginner, aligned to A1 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand and use familiar everyday expressions and very basic phrases aimed at the satisfaction of needs of a concrete type' — a learner here is able to introduce themselves and others, to ask and answer questions about personal details such as where they live, people they know and things they have, and to interact in a simple way provided the other person talks slowly and clearly and is prepared to help. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: Vietnam's own framework for learners of Vietnamese publishes no graded word list, and neither does any exam board, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 343 of the 500 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — greetings and politeness, the kinship words Vietnamese uses as pronouns, introducing yourself, family, numbers, telling the time, days and months, food and drink, shopping and money, the home, the town and getting about, the body and feeling ill, the weather, colours, the commonest classifiers, and the question words, particles and conjunctions every sentence is built out of — and the other 157 are the commonest remaining words of everyday Vietnamese, counted in film and television subtitles. Vietnamese writes a space between syllables rather than between words, so the subtitles were divided into words against the dictionary first, and a two-syllable word such as học sinh (pupil) is counted as one word. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. Beneath every headword its tones are named, one per syllable — ngang (no mark), huyền (à), sắc (á), hỏi (ả), ngã (ã) and nặng (ạ) — read off the marks the word is spelt with. 55 nouns show their classifier, the word that stands between a number and the noun (hai con mèo, two cats), and 97 words borrowed from Chinese show the characters they come from. The pronunciation is given in IPA for Hanoi and, where it differs, for Saigon. Real example sentences come with 499 of the 500 words, three apiece for 496 of them, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Spellings are Wiktionary's, which often puts the tone mark in the older place (hoà, khoẻ); the newer (hòa, khỏe) is equally correct. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, classifiers, characters and pronunciation: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: the OpenSubtitles 2018 Vietnamese text (opensubtitles.org, via the OPUS corpus collection), counted here. Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
